715.title: The harp (1 Samuel 16:14–23)
715.hook: young David plays, and the troubled king is refreshed
715.howItsDone: Christians sing and play music as part of worship, and some point to David playing for Saul when they talk about music as comfort for the troubled.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the youngest son came in from the sheep, and your line was god looks on the heart. Who did you give a second, longer look? Day seven hundred fifteen.

Yesterday's verses ended: the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward. The very next verse is hard to read beside it: "But the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD troubled him." One young man filled. One king emptied, and tormented. Saul's servants see it happening. Nothing says they know about the oil in Bethlehem. What they can see is that their king is not well, and they have an idea. Find a man who can play the harp, they say, and when the trouble comes on you, he'll play with his hand, "and thou shalt be well."

Start with the hard phrase: an evil spirit from the LORD. Readers have wrestled with it. Some understand it as a real spiritual being that God permits to trouble Saul. Others read it as the text's way of saying that Saul's own darkness, his fear and his rage, became a kind of judgment. Some modern readers hear in it something like deep anguish or depression, though the text doesn't use our words, and gives no diagnosis. Whatever it is, it comes in waves, and it hurts. Then one servant speaks up with a name. "I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, that is cunning in playing." Cunning here just means skilled. He keeps going: brave, a man of war, prudent in matters, a comely person, and, he adds, the LORD is with him. So Saul sends to Jesse: "Send me David thy son, which is with the sheep." The anointed boy walks into the court of the king he'll replace, with a donkey laden with bread, a bottle of wine and a young goat from his father. And the text says Saul loved him greatly, and made him his armor bearer. Nothing in the text says Saul knows who he's hired. The Hebrew word for the instrument is kinnor, a stringed instrument; the King James says harp, and some modern translations say lyre. Then the chapter's last verse, which gives the day its line: "when the evil spirit from God was upon Saul, that David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him." Refreshed. No speech, no argument, no fix for what was wrong. Just a boy, a few strings, and a tormented man able to breathe again, for now.
screen: `CUNNING IN PLAYING, AND THE LORD WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: play or listen to calming music. If you can, put on one quiet piece now, or play something yourself, or hum. If you can't, listen to the quietest sounds around you as if they were music. Settle, and breathe. Don't analyze it. Let it do what David's playing did, and give you a little room to breathe. If you pray, the Psalms are there to borrow. Music can help; when the trouble is heavy, it isn't the only help, and reaching for a person is part of the cure too. The bell holds the time.
The harp. David's kinnor in Saul's court. When the trouble came on the king, David played with his hand, and Saul was refreshed, and was well.
Your line: music can heal. Today, when the day gets heavy, put on one song before you reach for anything else, or send one to someone who's struggling. Day seven hundred fifteen.

what it means: a shepherd's stringed kinnor that let a tormented king breathe again.

716.title: Five smooth stones (1 Samuel 17)
716.hook: a shepherd refuses the king's armor and faces the giant with a sling
716.howItsDone: Christians tell the story of David and Goliath to children and adults alike, and read David's words, I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, as trust in God rather than in weapons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the harp, and your line was music can heal. When the day got heavy, did you reach for a song, or send one? Day seven hundred sixteen.

Two armies on two hills, a valley between them, and morning and evening a champion walks out from the Philistine side. Goliath of Gath, in a helmet of brass and a coat of mail, with a spear like a weaver's beam. "I defy the armies of Israel this day; give me a man, that we may fight together." Nobody goes. The text says Saul and all Israel were dismayed, and greatly afraid. Meanwhile a shepherd boy arrives from Bethlehem with grain and loaves for his older brothers, and cheeses for their captain. He hears the challenge, and he asks out loud who this Philistine is, "that he should defy the armies of the living God?" His eldest brother, Eliab, the one Samuel almost anointed, is furious with him. But the question gets back to the king.
screen: `A BOY WITH LOAVES FOR HIS BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: Saul looks at David and says what anyone would say. "Thou art not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him: for thou art but a youth." David answers with his résumé, and it's all sheep. A lion took a lamb, and he went after it. A bear too. "The LORD that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine." So Saul agrees, and does the kindest thing he knows. He dresses David in his own armor: a helmet of brass, a coat of mail, his sword. Notice whose armor that is. Saul stood higher than any of the people, and some readers point out that he was the obvious one to face the giant. Instead he hands his gear to a boy. David tries to walk in it, and stops. "I cannot go with these; for I have not proved them. And David put them off him." Proved means tested. It isn't that the armor is bad. It's that it's Saul's, and David has never fought in it. So he goes with what he has tested: "he took his staff in his hand, and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in a shepherd's bag." His sling in his hand. Five stones, and the text never says why five. When Goliath mocks him, David answers, "Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts." One stone is enough. It sinks into the giant's forehead, and he falls on his face. Then the narrator adds a quiet, pointed line: "there was no sword in the hand of David." Saul's sword was left behind with the borrowed armor.
screen: `THE LION, THE BEAR, AND THIS PHILISTINE.`
`NO SWORD IN THE HAND OF DAVID.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use your own tools, not someone else's. Settle, and breathe. Name one giant you're facing: a hard conversation, a project, a fear. Notice whose armor you've been trying to wear for it: someone else's way of talking, someone else's plan, a confidence that isn't yours. Then ask what's already in your bag. What have you tested? Patience, humor, honesty, a skill you learned in some small, unseen field. Choose one, the way David chose a stone. If you pray, you can bring the giant before God. The bell holds the time.
Five smooth stones. What the shepherd chose from the brook, after he put off Saul's armor. He needed one.
Your line: not in saul's armor. Today, face one hard thing your own way, with something you've already tested, and leave the borrowed armor by the brook. Day seven hundred sixteen.

717.title: Jonathan's love (1 Samuel 18:1–4; 20)
717.hook: the king's son gives David his robe and sword, and warns him with arrows
717.carry: a friend closer than a brother
717.howItsDone: Some Christians point to David and Jonathan as a picture of loyal friendship, and the story is read in sermons and small groups about friendship, loyalty and keeping promises.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five smooth stones, and your line was not in Saul's armor. What did you face with your own tools instead of borrowed ones? Day seven hundred seventeen.

A robe. A sword. A bow. A belt. That's the pile on the floor. The giant is dead, and the shepherd boy who killed him is standing in front of King Saul, still holding the head, answering questions about his father. And somewhere in that room is the king's son, Jonathan. A soldier himself, and the king's heir. He listens to David finish speaking. And then, before anyone has worked out what David will mean to this family, Jonathan takes off his own robe and hands it over. Then his garments. Then his sword, his bow and his belt. Today is about a friendship that started with someone giving away the clothes off his back.
screen: `A ROBE, A SWORD, A BOW, A BELT.`

segments.voice: Here is how the King James Bible opens chapter eighteen: "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Knit, like two threads worked into one cloth. Then the gift: "Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him, and gave it to David, and his garments, even to his sword, and to his bow, and to his girdle." Look at what those things are. A prince's robe. A prince's weapons. Some readers see more than generosity here. They see the heir quietly handing his rival the signs of the throne, long before anyone says it out loud. Then the friendship gets tested. Saul turns on David and wants him dead. Jonathan is caught between his father and his friend, and in chapter twenty the two of them set up a signal. Jonathan will go out to a field to practice with his bow, with a boy to fetch the arrows. If he calls to the boy that the arrows are on this side, David is safe. If he calls that the arrows are beyond him, David must run. The day comes. Jonathan shoots, and calls out, in the King James words: "Is not the arrow beyond thee?" It's a warning, and it's a goodbye. When the boy has gone, David comes out of hiding, and the text says they kissed one another and wept, and David wept the most. Jonathan sends him off in peace, with the promise they had made in the name of the Lord, binding them and their children after them. The Book of Proverbs has a line that fits these two: "there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother." Some Christians who teach on friendship turn to these two: a friendship that cost something.

Here's the practice: choose something of yours to give a friend. Settle, and breathe. Let one friend come to mind, someone who has stood with you when it cost them. Stay with their face for a moment. Then look around your life, not just your room: a book you love, a jacket, an hour of your time, a skill you could teach them, a word of thanks you've never said. Pick one thing that is really yours, not leftovers. If you pray, you can hold that friend before God in silence. If you don't, just keep their face in mind and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Jonathan's love. The king's son, knit to David soul to soul, who gave away his robe and sword and warned his friend with an arrow.
Your line: a friend closer than a brother. Today, give the thing you chose to the friend you thought of, or tell them when you will. Day seven hundred seventeen.

718.title: The cave (1 Samuel 24)
718.hook: David could kill Saul while he sleeps, and cuts only the edge of his robe
718.carry: I will not lift my hand
718.howItsDone: Some Christians read David sparing Saul in the cave alongside Jesus's teaching to love one's enemies, and the story is told in sermons and Sunday schools about refusing revenge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonathan's love: a robe, a sword, an arrow shot beyond a boy. Your line was a friend closer than a brother. What did you give? Day seven hundred eighteen.

Dark, cool, and very quiet. David and his men are crouched in the back of a cave in the wilderness of En-gedi, among the wild goats' rocks. Outside, King Saul is hunting him with an army. And then the king himself walks in, alone, to relieve himself, and has no idea who is sitting in the dark behind him. David's men can hardly breathe. One of them whispers what they're all thinking: this is the day the Lord promised, your enemy delivered into your hand. Do to him whatever seems good to you. David gets up. He creeps forward with a blade. And what he does next is today.

He cuts off a corner of Saul's robe. That's all. The king walks back out into the light and never feels it. And then a strange line, in the King James Bible: "David's heart smote him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt." Not for sparing him. For the cloth. Even that small cut felt like too much. He turns to his men and stops them cold: "The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD's anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him." Anointed is the key word. Saul was anointed king with oil, and David will not be the one to remove him, even after spears thrown at his head, even with a promise of the throne. Then David does something brave. He walks out of the cave after Saul and calls to him. He bows to the ground. He holds up the corner of the robe as proof: I was close enough to kill you, and I didn't. In his words: "I will not put forth mine hand against my lord; for he is the LORD's anointed." He leaves the judging to God. And Saul, the hunter, breaks. "Is this thy voice, my son David? And Saul lifted up his voice, and wept." He says it plainly: "Thou art more righteous than I." It doesn't last. Saul will hunt David again. The cave doesn't fix their story. What it shows is a man with every excuse and every chance, choosing not to take it. Some Christians read this chapter beside Jesus's teaching to love enemies and Paul's line in Romans about leaving vengeance to God. The robe corner is the whole lesson: proof of what you could have done.

For the next two minutes, find one chance to get even, and set it down. Breathe out slowly first. Let your mind go to someone who has wronged you, in a small way or a large one. Notice the chance you have, or could make: a remark you could repeat, a favor you could withhold, a story you could tell. Notice how sharp the blade is. Then picture David lowering his hand, holding only a scrap of cloth. You don't have to forgive everything today. Just decide not to cut. If you pray, you can hand the judging to God in silence. The bell holds the time.
The cave. In the dark at En-gedi, David spares the king who is hunting him, and takes only the corner of his robe.
Your line: I will not lift my hand. Today, when the chance to get even shows up, let it walk back out of the cave. Day seven hundred eighteen.

719.title: Abigail (1 Samuel 25)
719.hook: a wise woman rides out with bread and figs and talks David out of revenge
719.howItsDone: Some Christians tell Abigail's story as an example of courageous peacemaking and wise speech, and it is read in Bible studies about anger, conflict and the gift of a wise friend.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cave, and your line was I will not lift my hand. Did a chance to get even come along, and did you let it go? Day seven hundred nineteen.

Yesterday David spared a king. Today he nearly kills a farmer over a rude reply. The farmer is Nabal, a rich man with three thousand sheep, shearing them in Carmel. David's men have been out in the fields with Nabal's shepherds and kept them safe, and now David sends ten young men to ask, politely, for whatever Nabal can spare for a feast day. Nabal sneers. Who is David? There are plenty of runaway servants these days. Why should I give my bread to men I don't know? The messengers come back and report. David gives one order: every man, gird on your sword. About four hundred of them strap on swords and set out. Somebody needs to get in the way.

One of Nabal's servants runs to Nabal's wife, Abigail. The text calls her a woman of good understanding, and her husband churlish and evil in his doings. She doesn't argue with her husband. She doesn't wait. She loads donkeys: two hundred loaves, two bottles of wine, five sheep ready dressed, parched corn, a hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs. She sends them ahead, and rides out after them, and she tells Nabal nothing. On a hillside path she meets David coming down with his army. She gets off her donkey and bows to the ground. Then she speaks. She takes the blame on herself. She says her husband is just like his name: "as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him." And then she says the thing David needs to hear: when you are king one day, don't let this be a stumbling block on your conscience, that you shed blood without cause, that you avenged yourself with your own hand. She isn't only saving her household. She's saving David from himself. And David hears it. In the King James Bible: "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me: And blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand." Notice who he blesses. God, for sending her. Her advice. And her. In the cave, David held himself back. Here, someone else had to hold him back, and he was humble enough to let her. Later in the chapter Nabal dies, and David asks Abigail to be his wife.

Here's the practice: get ready to talk someone out of a rash act. Settle, and breathe. Is anyone near you riding down a hillside right now, with their sword on? A friend about to send an angry message. A family member about to quit, or storm off, or say the thing that can't be unsaid. Picture them. Then think the way Abigail did. Not how to win the argument, but what would help them see their better self. What could you bring? Bread first, words second. If you pray, you can ask for her kind of wisdom in your own words. If not, just picture the meeting on the path. The bell holds the time.
Abigail. Nabal's wise wife, who rode out with bread and figs and turned David back from shedding blood.
Your line: blessed be your wisdom. Today, if someone stops you from a rash act, thank them out loud, the way David did. Day seven hundred nineteen.

720.title: How are the mighty fallen (2 Samuel 1)
720.hook: David weeps for Saul, who hunted him, and for Jonathan
720.howItsDone: Some Christians read David's lament for Saul and Jonathan as a model of honest grief, and lines from it are sometimes read at funerals and memorials.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abigail on the hillside path, and your line was blessed be your wisdom. Who stopped you, or whom did you stop? Day seven hundred twenty.

A man runs into David's camp with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. He has come from the battle on Mount Gilboa, and he's carrying two things: a crown and a bracelet. Saul's. The king is dead, he says, and Jonathan with him. Saul hunted David through caves and wilderness. Now the throne is open. A man in David's position might feel relief. And here's what David does, in the text: he takes hold of his own clothes and tears them, and so do all the men with him. They mourn, and weep, and fast until evening, for Saul, and for Jonathan, and for the people. Then David sings.

The song is a lament, and the text says it is written in the book of Jasher. Its refrain is today's word, in the King James Bible: "The beauty of Israel is slain upon thy high places: how are the mighty fallen!" Listen to what he does next. He doesn't want the news spread among the enemy: "Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Askelon." He curses the mountains where they fell. And then he praises Saul. Not a word about the spears, the caves, the running. He tells the women of Israel to weep over Saul, who clothed them in scarlet. He sings of Saul and Jonathan together: "Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided: they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions." That's a hard thing to sing about a man who tried to kill you. Some readers call it generous. Some call it political: a new king honoring the old one. The text doesn't settle it. What it does is let David grieve the whole man, the king he was, not only the enemy he became. Then the song turns personal: "I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful." Two kinds of grief sit side by side in one song. Clean grief for a friend. And tangled grief for someone who did harm, and was also brave, and was also family. The refrain comes back at the end: how are the mighty fallen. One song, big enough to hold both.
screen: `A LAMENT, WRITTEN IN THE BOOK OF JASHER.`
`DAVID PRAISES THE MAN WHO HUNTED HIM.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to grieve someone complicated. Sit still for a moment first. Let one person come to mind whose loss is tangled: someone who hurt you and also gave you something, a parent, a friend you fell out with, someone gone whom you never quite made peace with. If no one comes, choose someone whose life you're grieving even while they're alive. Don't tidy them up. Let both be true at once. Then do what David did: find one honest good thing to say about them. Just one. If you pray, you can hold them before God without a verdict. The bell holds the time.
How are the mighty fallen. David's lament for Saul, who hunted him, and for Jonathan, who loved him.

721.title: Dancing before the ark (2 Samuel 6:12–16)
721.hook: the king dances with all his might, and his wife is embarrassed
721.tomorrow: A seat at the king's table
721.howItsDone: Some churches point to David dancing before the ark when they welcome dance, clapping and raised hands in worship, while others read it mainly as a lesson about humility and the heart behind worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how are the mighty fallen: David's song for Saul and Jonathan. What good thing did you say about someone complicated? This week walked from a harp and five stones to a crown. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

Six paces. That's how far the bearers carry it before David sacrifices, oxen and fatlings, the King James says. Then the procession moves on. David is king now, and he is bringing the ark of God, the sacred chest of the covenant, up into Jerusalem, his new city. There are trumpets. There is shouting. And at the front, out ahead of everyone, the king is not walking with dignity. He's dancing. Leaping and dancing, the text says, in a plain linen garment. And above the street, at a window in the palace, one person is watching who is not dancing at all: his wife Michal, the daughter of Saul.

Here is the verse, in the King James Bible: "And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod." With all his might. The King James uses the same English words for Samson bringing down the pillars, though the Hebrew behind them differs, and here they describe a king's joy. And the linen ephod matters. It was a simple linen garment, the kind the boy Samuel wore while serving at the sanctuary. The text says nothing here of a king's robe. Some readers see a king dressed for service, not for show. Then the camera moves to the window: "Michal Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart." It's easy to make Michal the villain here, and the text is fairer than that. She loved David once. She saved his life by letting him down through a window. Then she was given to another man while David was away, and brought back to David later. Her father and brothers are dead. She has her own reasons to watch from a window. But when she meets David afterward, she mocks him for uncovering himself in front of the servant girls like a fool. And David answers: it was before the LORD. "I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight." In other words, I'll look even sillier than this if that's what worship takes. Some Christians read this chapter as permission for joy that looks undignified: hands raised, clapping, dancing in church. Others hear a quieter point about the heart: what matters is who the dance is for. Either way, the king forgot to look like a king.

Here's the practice: dance, even a little. Nobody is watching from a window. Settle, and breathe. If you can stand, stand. If not, stay where you are. Let a song you love start playing in your head, any song with joy in it. Then move something: your hands, your shoulders, your head, your feet. Small is fine. Silly is fine. Let your body be glad for a minute, without checking how it looks. If you pray, you can make it a dance before God, as David did. If you don't, let it be a dance of thanks for being alive today.
